title: Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at loss-making subsidiary
text:
Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs | Lianhe Zaobao 
 Singapore International China Business Opinion Lifestyle Entertainment Search Published / 20 Nov 2026 18:43 S M L XL Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at loss-making subsidiary
 AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here. 
 Germany’s Deutsche Lufthansa AG, Europe’s largest airline group, plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its core namesake subsidiary, Lufthansa Airlines, according to Bloomberg. （AFP） Germany’s Deutsche Lufthansa AG, Europe’s largest airline group, plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its core namesake subsidiary, Lufthansa Airlines , as high fuel costs add to operating pressures and it seeks to return the mainline business to profit. 
 Bloomberg reported on Friday (20 November), citing a management letter to staff it had seen, that the company would cut full-time positions at its Munich and Frankfurt hubs. 
 Lufthansa also plans to further reduce capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and shrink its Airbus A320 fleet, switching to smaller Airbus A220 aircraft. 
 This is the company’s second round of job cuts in just over a year, underscoring the steep challenges the group faces in reviving its flagship brand. In September last year, Lufthansa Group announced plans to cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030. 
 Lufthansa is pursuing its biggest cost-cutting and efficiency drive in years, as high jet fuel prices and weakness in its core mainline business weigh on overall results. 
 Figures show that Lufthansa Airlines recorded an operating loss of €180 million (about S$260 million) in the first nine months of this year. 
 Management wrote in the letter: “After two years of transforming the business, we have to acknowledge that our existing measures are no longer sufficient to secure the company’s future. In fact, 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, persistently high fuel costs and a total of nine days of strikes, on top of our already extremely high cost base, have made the situation even more difficult.” 
 Lufthansa’s new supervisory board chairman, Johannes Teyssen, also said earlier this year that the company might need to do more to improve its weak performance, after earlier “self-inflicted damage” allowed rivals to erode its market share. 
 According to Bloomberg, Lufthansa announced the changes on Friday as it sought to resolve labour disputes with unions, although no agreement has yet been reached.
